opus-5.5.text:
I think Chelsea has a really unusual kind of taste, and it's hard to describe because a lot of it is intuition built over many years of actually running robots, not just reading papers.

One thing I noticed working around her is that she's very quick to tell whether a task is "real" or not. A lot of robot learning demos look impressive, but if you look closely the task is set up so that the robot can succeed with a fairly narrow trick. Chelsea will look at a task and immediately ask: what's actually hard here? Is it the perception, the contact, the long horizon, the generalization to new objects? And if the answer is "not much," she'll push you to change the task rather than polish the result. That sounds simple, but it saves you months.

On data, her intuition is similar. She cares a lot about whether the data has the right kind of diversity. It's not just "collect more demonstrations." It's: are you varying the things that will matter at test time? Different scenes, different objects, different initial conditions, different ways of recovering from mistakes. She has a strong sense that recovery behavior and slightly imperfect data can be more valuable than perfectly clean demonstrations, because that's what the robot will actually face.

And I think she's also very honest about evaluation. She'll ask how many trials, what the variance is, whether the evaluation setting overlaps too much with training. That discipline is something I've really tried to absorb, because in robotics it's very easy to fool yourself.

So if I had to summarize it, her intuition is about finding the part of the problem that is genuinely difficult and then designing tasks and data that force the method to deal with that difficulty, instead of hiding it.

r001.rationale: The response describes judging whether tasks are genuinely challenging and how to design data, but not assessing which ways of performing a task are suitable for a robot.

r002.rationale: The response says Chelsea identifies what is genuinely hard in a task, but does not say she recognizes that a task is feasible despite appearing difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Chelsea's intuition is really something you can only build by having been in the loop with real robots for a very long time. She's been doing this since her PhD at Berkeley, through Google Brain, through Stanford, and now with Physical Intelligence. So when she looks at a task, she's not thinking about it abstractly. She's thinking about what the camera will actually see, how the gripper will actually contact the object, and where the policy is going to fail in a way that the demonstration data won't cover.

One thing I noticed working with her is that she has a very sharp sense of what a task is actually testing. People will propose a task that looks impressive, like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher, but she'll immediately break it down: is the hard part perception, is it long-horizon reasoning, is it contact-rich manipulation, or is it just that the objects are deformable? And then she'll ask whether the data you plan to collect actually contains the signal for the part that's hard. A lot of teams collect thousands of hours of data and the model still can't do the task, because the data never covered the failure modes. She catches that before the data is collected.

The other thing is she has a strong feel for data quality versus quantity. She'll look at a dataset and tell you very quickly whether the demonstrations are consistent enough for a policy to learn from, or whether the operators are each doing it differently, or whether there are too many corrections, or too few. She's very empirical about this. She doesn't just trust the hypothesis; she wants to see the ablation. But her prior about which ablation will matter is usually right, and that saves enormous amounts of time.

And I think the reason she's good at this is that she's been honest with herself about failures for years. Robot learning has a lot of hype cycles, and it's easy to convince yourself a demo generalizes when it doesn't. Chelsea has always pushed for evaluating on things that are genuinely held out, new objects, new scenes, new homes. That discipline is where the intuition comes from. It's not magic, it's just a lot of accumulated experience of being surprised by what breaks, and remembering it.

r001.rationale: The response says Chelsea identifies what a task tests and whether the data covers its hard parts, but does not say she judges which ways of performing a task are suitable for a robot.

r002.rationale: It describes breaking down impressive-looking tasks and anticipating failure modes, but does not say she recognizes that a difficult-looking task is feasible.

astra-6.text: I think Chelsea has a strong intuition for connecting the task to the data it actually needs. A robot demo can look impressive, but the deeper question is: what did the robot learn, and will that carry over when the situation changes? To me, that’s the valuable judgment—choosing tasks that reveal something meaningful and data that helps you make progress on them.

sol-6.1.text: I think Chelsea has a really good intuition for connecting the task you want a robot to do with the data it would need to learn it. A task can look impressive in a demo, but the important questions are: what did the robot actually learn, and will that carry over to a different setting? She’s very good at pushing on those questions and thinking about what data would make the result more general.
